# Indriyabhāvanā Sutta (MN 152 (PTS MN iii 298))

**ID:** MN 152 (PTS MN iii 298)  
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Indriyabhāvanā Sutta  
**Title (English, from literature):** The Development of the Faculties  
**PTS:** MN iii 298  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul4.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul4.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Indriyabhāvanā Sutta* (MN 152) is the final discourse of the *Majjhima Nikāya*, delivered while the Buddha was staying at Kajangalā in a grove of mukhelu trees [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The discourse opens with a dialogue between the Buddha and the young brahmin student Uttara, a pupil of Pārāsariya (or Pārāsiya) [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Anālayo 2017; Polak 2011]. When asked how his teacher instructs disciples in the cultivation of the sense faculties (*indriyabhāvanā*), Uttara explains that one simply avoids seeing forms with the eye and hearing sounds with the ear [Hazra 1994; Anālayo 2017; Polak 2011]. The Buddha responds critically that, by such a standard, the blind and the deaf would be accomplished masters of sensory cultivation [Hazra 1994; Anālayo 2017; Anālayo 2019]. Following this, Ānanda intervenes—marking his final appearance in the *Majjhima Nikāya*—and requests that the Buddha expound the noble cultivation of the faculties [Freedman 1977].

In response, the Buddha explains the "supreme development of the faculties" (*anuttarā indriyabhāvanā*) and the arahant's mastery over perceptions [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Wen]. Rather than attempting the suppression or stoppage of sensory perception, noble cultivation entails experiencing sensory contact at the six sense doors without reactivity: recognizing liking or disliking as conditioned and dependently arisen, quickly abandoning them, and establishing unshakeable equanimity (*upekkhā*) [Polak 2011; Wen].

A full parallel is extant in Chinese translation in the *Saṃyuktāgama* (SĀ 282), alongside Sanskrit fragments identified as SHT sutta70. Anālayo notes that while the Pali discourse has the Buddha present both the blind and deaf counter-examples, SĀ 282 depicts Ānanda stepping in to supply the example of the deaf [Anālayo 2017]. The discourse is also cited in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* (*Iddhikathā*, Ps 3.2).

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: SA 282 諸根修; SHT Sutta 70
- Mentioned in: Ps 3.2 Iddhikathā

**Sources**

- [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995] Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Middle Length Discourses of the Buddha (1995) — Details on the setting at Kajangalā, interlocutors Uttara and Pārāsariya, and discourse summary.
- [Freedman 1977] Michael Freedman, The Characterization of Ānanda in the Pāli Canon of the Theravāda: A Hagiographic Study (1977) — Noted that this is Ānanda's last appearance in the Majjhima Nikāya and recorded his prompt to the Buddha.
- [Anālayo 2017] Bhikkhu Anālayo, A Meditator's Life of the Buddha (2017) — Account of the debate regarding avoiding sensory input, the blind/deaf counter-argument, and comparison with SĀ 282.
- [Anālayo 2019] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Mindfulness of Breathing: A Practice Guide and Translations (2019) — Analysis of the blind and deaf critique and the principle of dropping reactivity to sense experience.
- [Hazra 1994] Kanai Lal Hazra, Pāli Language and Literature (1994) — Summary of the discourse's critique of the brahmanical practice of faculty development.
- [Polak 2011] Grzegorz Polak, Reexamining Jhāna: Towards a Critical Reconstruction of Early Buddhist Soteriology (2011) — Analysis of the critique of Pārāsariya's practice and discussion of indriyabhāvanā as not stopping the senses.
- [Wen] Tzungkuen Wen, A Study of Sukkhavipassaka in Pāli Buddhism — Explanation of anuttarā indriyabhāvanā, noting like and dislike as conditioned, and establishing equanimity.
